title: FIR Design by Windowing
description: Design linear-phase FIR filters by windowing the ideal impulse response: Gibbs ripples, window trade-offs and Kaiser's design formulas.

study.title: Explore: the ideal low-pass filter
study.body: The ideal low-pass filter with cutoff $\omega_c$ and a delay of $\alpha$ samples has a sinc-shaped impulse response: infinitely long in both directions, so not realizable. **Window design** keeps only the samples $0 \le n \le M$ with $\alpha = M/2$ and multiplies them by a window $w[n]$. Symmetry about $M/2$ is kept, so the result has linear phase (type I or II). Drag the cutoff: a wider pass band gives a narrower main pulse (here $M = 20$).

study.title: Explore: truncation and the Gibbs phenomenon
study.body: Truncating is multiplying by a rectangular window, which convolves the ideal response with the window's transform $W(e^{j\omega})$. Its main lobe smears the jump into a **transition band**; its side lobes become **ripples** in both bands. The peak overshoot stays at about 9 % (stop band about −21 dB) however long the filter: a larger $M$ only squeezes the ripples towards the band edge. Drag $M$ to see it.

study.title: Tapered windows
study.body: Windows that taper smoothly to the ends have much lower side lobes, at the price of a wider main lobe. The classic ones are sums of cosines, defined for $0 \le n \le M$ (zero outside). Hann and Blackman reach zero at the ends; Hamming keeps a small pedestal of 0.08, chosen to cancel the first side lobe.

study.title: Main lobe versus side lobes
study.body: The window **shape** fixes the side-lobe level and hence the ripple $\delta$ of the filter (the same in pass and stop band); the **length** $M$ sets the main-lobe width and hence the transition width. Main-lobe widths of the windows: $4\pi/(M+1)$ (rectangular), $8\pi/M$ (Hann, Hamming) and $12\pi/M$ (Blackman). The transition width $\Delta\omega$ of the designed filter, measured between the band edges where the error equals $\delta$, is smaller: about $1.8\pi/M$, $6.2\pi/M$, $6.6\pi/M$ and $11\pi/M$. These are our own measurements, not values from the table in O&S, which lists the main-lobe widths. Peak side lobes of the windows: −13, −31, −41 and −57 dB. Explore the filters: the orange line is the stop-band level in the table.

study.title: The Kaiser window
study.body: The Kaiser window has a shape parameter $\beta$ that trades side-lobe level against main-lobe width continuously ($I_0$ is the modified Bessel function of order 0; $\beta = 0$ is rectangular). Kaiser found empirical design formulas: from the ripple $\delta$ (the smaller of $\delta_1$, $\delta_2$) and the transition width $\Delta\omega = \omega_s - \omega_p$ you get $\beta$ and $M$ directly. Below 21 dB, $\beta = 0$.

study.title: Explore: Kaiser window design
study.body: $w[n] = I_0\big(\beta\sqrt{1 - ((n - \alpha)/\alpha)^2}\big)/I_0(\beta)$ with $\alpha = M/2$. Raise $\beta$: the stop band goes down (about 9 dB per unit of $\beta$ once $\beta > 4.5$), but the transition gets wider. Then raise $M$ to narrow the transition again. The cutoff here is $\omega_c = \pi/2$.

study.title: Worked example: Kaiser design
study.body: Specs: pass band to $\omega_p = 0.3\pi$, stop band from $\omega_s = 0.45\pi$, $\delta_1 = \delta_2 = 0.005$. Then $A = -20\log_{10}0.005$ = 46.0 dB, so $\beta = 0.5842 \cdot 25.0^{0.4} + 0.07886 \cdot 25.0$ = 4.09. $\Delta\omega = 0.15\pi$ = 0.471 rad gives $M = 38.0/(2.285 \cdot 0.471)$ = 35.3, so $M = 36$ (37 taps). The cutoff goes in the middle of the transition band: $\omega_c = 0.375\pi$. Checking the result: ripple 0.0040 in the pass band and 0.0045 in the stop band, within spec.

study.title: High-pass and band-pass by windowing
study.body: Any ideal response can be windowed. A **high-pass** is an all-pass delay minus a low-pass: $h_d[n] = \delta[n - \alpha] - h_{LP}[n]$; this needs an integer $\alpha$ (even $M$, type I), since type II has a forced zero at $\omega = \pi$. A **band-pass** is the difference of two low-passes with cutoffs $\omega_2 > \omega_1$. Window the result with the same window and the same $M$.

steps.title: The ideal low-pass filter
steps.body: An ideal low-pass filter with cutoff $\omega_c$ and a delay of $\alpha$ samples has a sinc impulse response that never ends. Window design delays it by $\alpha = M/2$, keeps only $0 \le n \le M$ and multiplies by a window. The centre tap is $\omega_c/\pi$; the other taps oscillate and fall off as $1/(n - \alpha)$. Drag the cutoff.

steps.prompt: A low-pass filter with $\omega_c = {{wcp}}\pi$ is designed with a rectangular window and $M$ = {{M}}, so $h[n] = h_d[n]$ for $0 \le n \le {{M}}$.

ask.explanation: At $n = \alpha = M/2$ = {{M/2}} the sinc is 0/0; its limit is $\omega_c/\pi$ = {{wcp}}.
$n - \alpha$ = {{k}}: $h = \frac{\sin(\omega_c \cdot {{k}})}{\pi \cdot {{k}}}$ = sin({{pi*wcp*k||3}} rad) / {{pi*k||3}} = {{sin(pi*wcp*k)/(pi*k)||3}}. By symmetry $h[{{M/2-k}}]$ is the same.

steps.title: Truncation causes ripples
steps.body: Cutting off the sinc is multiplying by a rectangular window. In frequency this convolves the ideal response with the window's transform: the jump is smeared into a transition band and ripples appear on both sides. Drag $M$: the ripples crowd towards the edge, but the overshoot stays at about 9 %.

steps.prompt: Doubling the order $M$ of a rectangular-window design halves the peak overshoot near the band edge.
steps.explanation: This is the **Gibbs phenomenon**: the overshoot is set by the area of the window transform's side lobes, about 9 % of the jump (a stop band of only −21 dB), whatever $M$ is. A longer filter narrows the transition band and squeezes the ripples towards the edge, but they keep their height. Only a different window shape lowers them.

steps.prompt: Why is the ideal impulse response delayed by $\alpha = M/2$ before it is truncated to $0 \le n \le M$?
options: To make the filter causal while keeping it symmetric, so it has linear phase
To make the DC gain exactly 1
To halve the width of the transition band
steps.explanation: $h_d[n]$ is symmetric about $n = \alpha$. Centring it in the window $0 \ldots M$ keeps the most significant (central) samples and keeps $h[n] = h[M - n]$: a causal filter with generalized linear phase and a delay of $M/2$ samples. The delay changes nothing about the ripples or the transition width.

steps.title: Main lobe and side lobes
steps.body: Two properties of the window decide the filter: its **main-lobe width** sets the transition width (shrinks as $1/M$), its **side-lobe level** sets the ripple (fixed by the shape). For the rectangular window the main lobe is $4\pi/(M+1)$ wide; the measured transition width of the filter is narrower, about $1.8\pi/M$.

steps.prompt: A rectangular window has order $M$ = {{M}}, and the filter runs at $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: Find the main-lobe width of the window's transform, in rad/sample.
ask.explanation: $\Delta\omega_{ml} = \frac{4\pi}{M + 1}$ = 4π / {{M+1}} = {{4*pi/(M+1)|rad}}: the distance between the first nulls on either side of the peak.

ask.prompt: Find the main-lobe width in Hz.

steps.prompt: Match each window with the stop-band attenuation of the low-pass filter it gives.
steps.explanation: The smoother the taper, the lower the side lobes and the deeper the stop band, but the wider the main lobe and the transition band. These values do not depend on $M$.

steps.title: Tapered windows
steps.body: Tapering the ends removes the abrupt jump of the rectangular window. The side lobes drop, the main lobe widens. All of these are defined for $0 \le n \le M$.

steps.prompt: A specification asks for at least 50 dB of stop-band attenuation. Which fixed window gives the shortest filter for a given transition width?
steps.explanation: Hann (44 dB) and rectangular (21 dB) cannot reach 50 dB at any length. Both Hamming (53 dB) and Blackman (74 dB) can, but Hamming has the narrower transition: $\Delta\omega \approx 6.6\pi/M$ against $11\pi/M$. For the same $\Delta\omega$ the Blackman filter is about 1.7 times longer.

steps.title: Explore: comparing windows
steps.body: Pick a window and an order. The shape fixes the stop-band level (orange line); the order fixes the transition width. The $\Delta\omega$ column gives measured transition widths of the filters, not the main-lobe widths of the windows.

steps.prompt: A low-pass filter needs {{A}} dB of stop-band attenuation and a transition width of {{dw}}$\pi$. Choose the fixed window (Hann, Hamming or Blackman) that gives the shortest filter, and find the smallest order $M$. (Hann: 44 dB, $\Delta\omega \approx 6.2\pi/M$; Hamming: 53 dB, $6.6\pi/M$; Blackman: 74 dB, $11\pi/M$.)
steps.explanation: The window must reach {{A}} dB: Hann gives 44 dB, Hamming 53 dB, Blackman 74 dB. The shortest one that suffices has $\Delta\omega \approx$ {{C}}$\pi/M$. So $M \ge$ {{C}}π / ({{dw}}π) = {{C/dw||4}}, i.e. $M$ = {{ceil(C/dw - 1e-9)}}.

steps.prompt: A Hamming-window low-pass has $\omega_p = {{wp}}\pi$, $\omega_s = {{ws}}\pi$ and $\omega_c$ in the middle. Set the smallest order $M$ for which the response stays below −50 dB from $\omega_s$ on.
steps.explanation: For a Hamming window $\Delta\omega \approx 6.6\pi/M$. With $\Delta\omega$ = {{dw}}π: $M \approx 6.6/{{dw}}$ = {{6.6/dw||3}}, rounded to an even order. Below that the transition band spills past $\omega_s$; above it the filter is longer than needed. The stop-band level itself (about −53 dB) does not improve with $M$.

steps.prompt: Three low-pass filters with $M = 30$ and $\omega_c = \pi/2$ were designed with different windows (dB scale, −100 to 5 dB). Which one used the Blackman window?
steps.explanation: The Blackman window has the lowest side lobes, so its filter has the deepest stop band (about −74 dB), and the widest main lobe, so the slowest roll-off. The rectangular window gives the sharpest edge but only about −21 dB; Hann sits in between at about −44 dB.

steps.prompt: With a fixed window shape, a longer filter gives more stop-band attenuation.
steps.explanation: For a fixed shape the relative side-lobe area of the window, and so the ripple $\delta$, hardly depends on $M$. A longer filter only narrows the transition band. To get more attenuation you need a different shape: a Kaiser window with a larger $\beta$, for instance.

steps.title: Kaiser's design formulas
steps.body: The Kaiser window's parameter $\beta$ trades ripple against transition width continuously. Kaiser fitted formulas that turn the specifications directly into $\beta$ and $M$: use the smaller ripple $\delta = \min(\delta_1, \delta_2)$ and the transition width $\Delta\omega = \omega_s - \omega_p$ in rad/sample.

steps.prompt: Find the Kaiser window parameter $\beta$ for a ripple of {{A}} dB ($A$ = {{A}}).
Find the Kaiser window parameter $\beta$ for $A$ = {{A}} dB.
Kaiser design: pass band up to $\omega_p = {{wp}}\pi$, stop band from $\omega_s = {{wp+dw}}\pi$, $\delta_1 = \delta_2$ = {{d}}.

ask.prompt: Find the cutoff $\omega_c$ of the ideal response, in rad/sample.
ask.explanation: Put the cutoff in the middle of the transition band, where the windowed response passes 0.5: $\omega_c = (\omega_p + \omega_s)/2$ = {{(2*wp+dw)/2}}π = {{pi*(2*wp+dw)/2|rad}}.

steps.prompt: The graph shows a Kaiser-window low-pass with $M = 40$. Set $\beta$ for a stop band at −{{A}} dB, using Kaiser's formula (and check the graph).
steps.explanation: $A$ = {{A}}: $\beta$ = {{bt||3}} (for $A > 50$: $0.1102(A - 8.7)$; for $21 \le A \le 50$: $0.5842(A-21)^{0.4} + 0.07886(A-21)$). The side lobes then just touch the −{{A}} dB line. A larger $\beta$ lowers them further but widens the transition band.

steps.prompt: A Kaiser design must keep the pass-band gain within $1 \pm$ {{d1}} and the stop-band gain below {{d2}}. Which value of $A$ do you use in the design formulas?
steps.explanation: A window design gives (nearly) the same ripple $\delta$ in both bands, so it must meet the stricter one: $\delta = \min$({{d1}}, {{d2}}) = {{min(d1,d2)}}, and $A = -20\log_{10}\delta$ = {{-20*log10(min(d1,d2))|dB}}. The other band is then better than required: a waste that optimal (equiripple) design avoids.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of a Kaiser-window low-pass design in order.
items: Convert the band edges to $\omega$ in rad/sample
Check the response; increase $M$ if a band edge is missed
steps.explanation: Everything follows from $\delta$ and $\Delta\omega$: $A$ gives $\beta$ (the shape) and, together with $\Delta\omega$, $M$ (the length). Only then can the ideal response be sampled and windowed. The formulas are empirical, so the final check sometimes asks for $M + 1$ or $M + 2$.

steps.require: min(min(M0 - floor(M0), ceil(M0) - M0) - 0.1, fs/2 - fp - tw)
steps.prompt: A Kaiser-window low-pass at $f_s$ = {{fs|Hz}} must pass up to {{fp|Hz}} and attenuate by {{A}} dB from {{fp+tw|Hz}}.

ask.prompt: Find the transition width $\Delta\omega$ in rad/sample.

steps.prompt: A high-pass filter is designed as $h[n] = \big(\delta[n - M/2] - h_{LP}[n]\big)w[n]$ with a Hamming window, $M$ = {{M}} and a low-pass cutoff $\omega_c = {{wcp}}\pi$.

ask.explanation: At the centre the window is 1 and $h_{LP}[M/2] = \omega_c/\pi$ = {{wcp}}: $h[{{M/2}}] = 1 - $ {{wcp}} = {{1-wcp}}.

$h_{LP}[M/2 + 1] = \sin(\omega_c)/\pi$ = {{sin(pi*wcp)/pi||4}}. The Hamming window one sample from the centre is $0.54 - 0.46\cos(2\pi \cdot {{M/2+1}}/{{M}})$ = {{w1||4}}. So $h$ = −{{w1||4}} × {{sin(pi*wcp)/pi||4}} = {{-w1*sin(pi*wcp)/pi||3}}.

steps.prompt: An ideal band-pass response from $\omega_1 = {{w1p}}\pi$ to $\omega_2 = {{w2p}}\pi$ is the difference of two ideal low-passes. With a rectangular window and delay $\alpha$:

ask.explanation: Each low-pass contributes $\omega_c/\pi$ at the centre: {{w2p}} − {{w1p}} = {{w2p-w1p}}, the width of the pass band as a fraction of $\pi$.

steps.prompt: Specs: {{A}} dB stop band, transition width {{dw}}$\pi$. A Hamming window ($\Delta\omega \approx 6.6\pi/M$) would do. How many fewer taps does a Kaiser design need?
steps.explanation: Hamming: $M = 6.6/{{dw}}$ → {{Mh}}, and it gives 53 dB, more than needed. Kaiser: $M = \frac{A - 8}{2.285\,\Delta\omega}$ = {{A-8}} / (2.285 × {{pi*dw||3}}) = {{Mk0||4}} → {{ceil(Mk0)}}. The Kaiser filter is {{Mh - ceil(Mk0)}} taps shorter, because its $\beta$ delivers exactly the {{A}} dB asked for.

steps.prompt: A Kaiser-window low-pass designed for $A$ = 60 dB of stop-band attenuation also keeps its pass-band gain within about ±0.1 %.
steps.explanation: Window designs have (nearly) equal ripple in both bands: $\delta = 10^{-60/20}$ = 0.001. In the pass band that is a gain between 0.999 and 1.001, i.e. ±0.1 % (±0.009 dB).

steps.prompt: A Hann-window low-pass with $M$ = 40 has the right transition width but only 44 dB of stop-band attenuation; 60 dB is needed. What should you change?
options: Use a Kaiser window with $\beta \approx 5.7$ and a larger $M$
Keep the Hann window and double $M$
Move $\omega_c$ further into the stop band
Use a rectangular window with a larger $M$
steps.explanation: The ripple is fixed by the window shape, so only a different shape helps: $A$ = 60 gives $\beta = 0.1102 \cdot 51.3$ = 5.65. Its wider main lobe widens the transition, so $M$ must grow to $52/(2.285\,\Delta\omega)$. Doubling $M$ with Hann only narrows the transition; moving $\omega_c$ trades pass band for stop band but keeps the ripple.
